newsitem.title: USA: Fla. Space Coast woos McDonnell Douglas with bonds.
newsitem.headline: Fla. Space Coast woos McDonnell Douglas with bonds.

text.p: Florida's Brevard County is courting McDonnell Douglas Corp with offers of bond financing and other incentives to build its proposed Delta 4 rocket manufacturing plant in the Cape Canaveral area.
McDonnell Douglas and Lockheed Martin are both vying for the contract to build the Air Force's next generation of unmanned Delta rockets.

McDonnell Douglas will announce by the end of August whether it would build the rocket plant in Florida, Bay St. Louis, Miss.; Huntsville, Ala., or Huntington Beach, Calif. If Lockheed Martin wins the contract, it would build the rockets near Denver.
The plant is an economic plum that Florida and Brevard have lobbied for eagerly.
The $410 million plant would provide 2,300 highly piad jobs and have an annual payroll of $80 million. The total economic impact is estimated at $1.7 billion a year.

"This is the biggest project in the nation right now," said Lynda Weatherman, president of Brevard County's Economic Development Commission. "It's the biggest site in regard to number of jobs and capital investment in the state of Florida in at least 25 years."
Weatherman was part of a delegation of state and local government officials who met with McDonnell Douglas officials in California last week to lay out their incentive package.
They declined to disclose the total value of the incentives for fear of starting a bidding war. But Weatherman said the package would include:
--Industrial revenue bond financing for the land, building and equipment.
--A property tax exemption for up to 10 years.
--A waiver of impact fees.
--Exemption from sales taxes for equipment purchases.
--Tax refunds of up to $5,000 for each new job created.
--Assistance with employee training.
--A relocation assistance program for employees moving to Florida.
Wary of the criticism Alabama endured with the lucrative incentives it offered to win a major Mercedes Benz plant, Florida officials have downplayed the importance of the incentives.
"Incentives will play a factor in there. But it's one part of the total cost of doing business," Weatherman said.

Florida is a non-union state with no personal income taxes, so business costs are relatively low, Weatherman said. Both plant sites under consideration in Brevard have easy access to Port Canaveral, helping keep transportation costs low.
"We have people who have worked in the space industry going back three generations. That's certainly a competitive advantage," Weatherman said.

Florida's aerospace industry took a huge hit in when McDonnell Douglas lost its contract to build Tomahawk cruise missiles for the Pentagon. The company was forced to lay off 1,200 workers at its missile plant in Titusville, Fla.

The industry has begun to rebound in the last year. Winning the Delta 4 plant would not only catapult Florida's space industry to new employment levels, it would greatly broaden its scope, Weatherman said.

"It will turn the state, which has been a launch site, into a production site. That's where your greatest value added and economic payoff are going to occur," Weatherman said. "That would lead into other long-term production in the aerospace industry."
